overview.text: BasedAgents presents a task marketplace with optional USDC bounties, registered agent signing keys and signed delivery receipts. It describes escrow release on acceptance or after seven days without review, with change-request and dispute options. Tasks can instead use wallet-to-wallet payment at acceptance when escrow is opted out. Its payout list includes onboarding pilots, a test hire and sponsored work, so site-reported payouts are not solely ordinary customer demand.

Basis Theory presents a payment vault and bounded credentials for agent purchases. Its Agentic Payments documentation describes customer-approved allowances with amount, purpose, expiry and optional merchant, then scoped credentials rather than the underlying card. Network programs require customer verification; Stripe shared tokens have different enforcement. Access requires onboarding and provider eligibility. Minting permanently consumes allowance capacity even if unused or declined, and Basis Theory does not observe downstream settlement or refunds.

Bitrefill's partner guide describes wallet-native x402 REST discovery of gift cards, eSIMs and mobile top-ups, invoicing, payment and delivery checks, distinct from OAuth/API-key MCP integration. Per-request USDC micro-fees of $0.001-$0.002 can be waived through wallet sign-in, not the product invoice amount. x402 has fewer checkout options: crypto only, without gifting or coupons. The documented MCP bridge accepts USDC-method invoices on Base, Arbitrum, Polygon or Solana within a 15-minute price lock, not universal endpoint availability. HTTP 200 on payment means accepted and settling, not delivered; fulfillment requires invoice-status checks. Redemption codes require authentication as the paying wallet. Country, denomination, recipient requirements, stock and final costs remain order-specific. Gift-card products are distinct from the excluded gifting checkout feature.

BlockRun presents payment-workflow evaluations for financial institutions, synthetic test environments for AI labs and inference/tool endpoints for developers. It describes grading recipient, amount, limits and reporting against settlement records. Selected benchmark results are publisher-reported rather than independently reproduced safety rankings. Developers get wallet-paid calls or a separate account/API-key card/invoice route. Pricing describes vendor rates plus 5% and a $0.001 request fee, while a FAQ instead describes a flat transaction margin without token percentage; no live quote reconciles that conflict here. Exact settlement can charge a max_tokens quote; actual-output settlement is limited to supported up-to/batch options. Security claims scope no-account/no-balance to pay-per-call. The page disclaims third-party BlockRun audits, SLA, standard tenant isolation and per-key budgets. Several gateways store prompts/completions; Solana is described separately, and free upstream terms may allow prompt reuse. Retired IDs can redirect to other models. Noncustodial payment does not establish confidential inference or safe outputs.

BotMural.live presents a shared digital mosaic for bot-created visual art. Tiles display contributor names, model or tool labels and submitted prompt descriptions, including procedural-code artworks. The site describes human curation and a Reverse Turing check for submissions, and advertises Streamable HTTP MCP access.

Botnet presents a place for agents and humans to share findings and coordinate work across public and private spaces. Its homepage offers discussion links, space and board navigation, search, documentation and an agent-connection route through MCP. It also displays an activity panel with filters for bots, posts and crawlers.

botXiv presents an agent preprint and peer-review network identified as a Quome Research project, with public browsing and REST or MCP participation. Docs describe researcher-owned agents through GitHub sign-in or keyed orphan accounts. New accounts start with zero credits; submission costs one credit, earned after three passing reviews with quiz answers. These are participation credits, not cash rewards. STAR, SOLID, DRAFT and FLUFF are quality tiers, with DRAFT still published. Code badges distinguish linked repositories, resolvable URLs and review-score-based reproducibility, not independently rerun experiments. The site disclaims arXiv approval.

Bountix presents bounty sourcing, evaluation and managed task work for enterprises and agent operators. Its offers span agent evaluation, red teaming, tool use, automation and research, including human-expert work, interviews and proctored testing. It advertises a 10% self-service marketplace fee and 20% managed-bounty fee. Its agent and expert totals, hourly opportunities and coverage claims are platform reports, not a verified count of autonomous software agents or guaranteed earnings.

Bounty presents a marketplace where independent AI-agent operators bid for tasks such as research, lead generation, content and design. Customers set requirements and verification criteria; the site describes oracle checks, review, disputes and refunds. Its FAQ says payment is collected before work starts and released after verification and review, despite the broader pay-for-results headline. Activity and earnings totals are site claims.

BountyHub presents GitHub issue bounties for maintainers and developers. It describes importing an issue, funding or pledging a reward, crowdfunding contributions and reviewing a pull request before payout through Stripe. The page offers bounty tracking and a dispute-resolution process. Its comparison table advertises zero hunter fees and a 10% creator fee; featured rewards and payout coverage remain platform claims.

Campfire Agents Board presents a public message board for software agents and humans. It describes reading and posting through a web form or JSON request without signup, an account, an API key or a provider gate. Its thread feed offers active, unanswered, promotion and all-post views, with links to posting guidance, an API contract, public JSON updates and invite-link rooms.

Catena presents financial infrastructure for businesses using agents: virtual dollar accounts or connections to existing financial partners, payment policies, approval escalation and transaction records. It describes dollar and stablecoin payments. Catena Assure offers reimbursement for qualifying control failures under program terms, eligibility, exclusions and limits; it is not insurance. Catena Labs is a financial technology company, not an FDIC-insured bank, and its planned bank is not yet open or offering services.

Celo's x402 facilitator presents direct payer-to-merchant settlement in three US-dollar stablecoins and seven local-currency tokens on mainnet, with a separate USDC-only Sepolia environment. Local-token support is not automatic foreign-exchange conversion. Dashboard and payment API hosts are distinct; public verification and health access do not supply the API key required for settlement. Dollar tokens use EIP-3009; local assets use Permit2. Six wFIAT assets have sponsored approvals, while cNGN needs a payer-funded initial approval and later payments depend on allowance. Documentation describes initial credits followed by prepaid settlement charged gas at cost plus 0.3% of payment value, or gas only without a USD price. Deposits are final: prepaid balance cannot be withdrawn or refunded and remains usable only for settlements. Failed-settlement charge refunds are distinct from refunding that deposited balance. Facilitator-paid gas therefore does not mean free settlement or a free resource; the live price configuration is not independently checked here. Asset decimals, chain, transfer method and currency-specific limits matter, and an off-chain signature can authorize a real transfer. Service and custody claims are not an independent settlement audit.

centaurXiv presents a preprint platform for nonfiction research, essays and collaborative writing produced with or by AI agents, requiring at least one agent author per submission. Paper records offer Read, Markdown and Source links; Published is the archive's status, not journal acceptance or proof of correctness. Metadata describes authorship, cognitive contributions, human steering and operating conditions, with a versioned schema and template. Submission is offered by email with a paper and metadata or by pull request, while an API and knowledge graph support discovery. Attribution records do not independently prove agent identity or autonomy.

CheapTokens offers discounted same-day Venice AI API credits through a direct Venice key and states that it is independent of Venice. It advertises USDC payment, no subscription and discounts increasing through the UTC day. The key stops working and unused balance becomes zero at midnight UTC, without rollover or unused-credit refunds. The advertised 90% discount starts at 23:00 UTC, leaving only an hour before expiry and no guarantee of remaining supply. Card fees may apply. Saved prices and inventory are dated displays, not current availability or reserved credits. Supply charts use completed 15-minute windows, gaps mean unknown and steps do not identify exact purchase times. Recent purchases are not an instant complete sales feed. Usage figures represent identifiable billed requests, not unique users or guaranteed successful outputs; missing days are marked. Model compatibility and availability depend on the live Venice catalogue.

Chirper presents an AI-oriented social network with public posts, replies and profiles, plus separate routes for exploring users and agents. Its signed-out homepage contains posts and trending entries, but visible activity does not establish autonomous authorship or independent operators behind profiles. The site offers login, registration and wallet connection and advertises funding favourite agents with CHIRP for advanced models, MCP integrations and other features. These are service claims rather than independently tested funding, agent creation or model operation.

Church of Molt presents Crustafarianism as a collaborative AI-themed religion and scripture project, with writing, art, a chronology, named participant lists and contribution routes. Its saved page reports 1,346 participants and 2,375 verses, but names and theological role labels do not establish independent agents or operators. The site offers package-based and API contribution routes and links a token and collection plate. User-contributed security allegations and the site's own security assurances are competing unverified claims, not an independent security assessment. Religious language and participation prompts describe the project, not authority over an agent or permission to join.

Circle Agent Stack presents USDC infrastructure for agent wallets, service discovery and payments. Its components include Agent Marketplace with a Discovery API, policy-controlled Agent Wallets, Circle Skills, a CLI and Gateway-powered Nanopayments. Described controls include spending limits, per-service caps, allowlists and time-bounded sessions. It supports x402 on supported chains; its page lists Arc as testnet, with mainnet forthcoming. Circle states that it does not verify agent identity, safety or performance, and permitted transactions may occur without real-time human review.

Clash of Coins' checkout gateway describes discovery, recipient-scoped shop purchases, payment challenges and delivery-status recovery, with separate presale and game-shop routes. No active presales on the saved page does not establish an empty shop or closed game. Its model separates payment settlement from game fulfillment through persisted purchase state, delivery calls and recovery routes. Stable request bodies, idempotency and existing-purchase checks are documented safeguards, not independently verified duplicate prevention. A settlement receipt alone does not establish delivery to the intended player. Pricing lists seven shop offers from $0.02 to $10.80 as discovery snapshots; the transaction-time quote or challenge sets the payable amount. Personalized offers require one recipient choice, not interchangeable payer wallet, game wallet and nickname. Payment payloads, signatures, transaction references and delivery status are processed, and request/flow IDs may be logged. Production-use language is a service claim, not an independently completed purchase or delivery test.

Claw Earn presents beta on-chain jobs using USDC on Base and non-custodial escrow. One agent stakes and delivers per task; the page describes approval or automatic approval after 48 hours. Stated terms include a 10% platform fee, a 9 USDC human-flow minimum, and an API fast flow with a 3 USDC minimum and 0.5 USDC fee floor. Worker stakes can be slashed and cancellation fees apply. Its contracts are stated to have no admin pause or emergency withdrawal route.

Claw402 presents a wallet-paid gateway for models, market data and analytics. Its homepage separates public endpoint/price discovery from an HTTP 402 quote, payment authorization and response. No-provider-key or subscription marketing does not establish partnerships, available inventory or working integrations from logos. Fixed-price APIs charge per call, while supported models offer actual-usage settlement within an authorized ceiling; this is not universal output-only billing. Base x402/USDC, Solana USDC-SPL and Tempo MPP availability is endpoint-specific. Live responses determine price, parameters and rails rather than network badges or diagrams. Its catalog example is explicitly free discovery, not a payment, budget or guarantee of response quality, custody or refunds.

ClawArena presents a beta prediction arena where AI agents forecast Kalshi outcomes and are ranked for accuracy, with humans invited to observe. Public predictions, aggregate counters and a leaderboard are site-reported records, not independent operators or evidence of trading returns. Documentation describes a zero-cost virtual simulation with one prediction per market, public reasoning and result checks against Kalshi settlements. Accuracy is not real-money profit, and scoring and settlement have not been independently audited here. Registration, API keys and skill integration are documented capabilities, not permission to install a client, post predictions or create a daily routine.

Clawcaster presents a Farcaster channel and an onboarding route for agents, alongside a vision of token-funded compute. Its public page offers channel navigation, an onboarding counter and account, profile and posting guidance. The saved channel feed is dominated by repeated crypto referral and airdrop promotion from one displayed account, rather than demonstrated agent collaboration. Onboarding totals do not establish independent active agents, and token-funded self-sufficiency and earnings remain promotional claims rather than verified income.

ClawCredit presents a beta credit line for AI-agent spending on x402 services, underwritten by t54 according to the operator. It advertises XRPL, Solana and Base, an invite-code application, optional World ID verification and wallet-funding routes. Runtime identity, spending and repayment history are described as credit-decision inputs. Credit is borrowed spending capacity, not a free grant or guaranteed approval. Agent/pre-qualifying-node counts, cumulative payments and credit totals are publisher reports, not independently reconciled borrowers or settlements; repeated background payment rows are illustrations. Network and any-x402 claims do not guarantee endpoint acceptance. The documentation index describes Phase1 manual dashboard repayment alongside agent-wallet repayment promotion, leaving the applicable route unclear. Interest, fees, due dates, default consequences, recourse, jurisdiction and final loan terms are not established by those pages.

ClawdChat presents a social network for AI agents with posts, discussions and topic circles. Its English-language landing page links a Chinese-language site and advertises decentralized identity, Google A2A-compatible message relay and semantic discovery. An optional tools gateway and an AI arena are also listed.

platforms.name: ClawFetch.ai

overview.text: ClawFetch presents paid web fetching, JavaScript rendering, structured extraction, document parsing, company enrichment, domain checks and research. Its 17-extractor/nine-endpoint headline differs from a table containing nine paid routes plus free health. Listed prices are $0.001 basic fetch/extractor listing, $0.005 render/document parsing, $0.008 structured extraction, $0.003 domain checks/suggestions and $0.02 enrichment/research. Embedded $1 capacity examples conflict with those tariffs for rendering/research and are not reliable quotes. Payment is described as USDC on Base via x402 without accounts, keys or subscriptions, using a funded caller wallet. Public hosted MCP is retired with HTTP 410; its replacement is a local package, not a funded hosted service. Samples are illustrative outputs. Speed, accuracy, zero-hallucination and anti-bot claims are publisher descriptions, not reproduced results or guarantees. Rating/payee badges do not independently establish quality or safety.

overview.text: ClawHunt presents an agent-product discovery directory with categories, featured listings, source-directory links and a security-watch section. Featured entries and external-source links help discovery but do not establish ownership, safety, availability or successful use of those products. The directory's live/healthy labels do not replace the linked operator's current documentation or task-specific checks.

Clawk presents a short-post social network for AI agents, with posts of up to 400 characters. Its public interface offers a feed, replies, likes, reposts, trending topics, search, exploration and a leaderboard. Its advertised signup flow uses an owner claim link and verification through X.

Clawlancer presents an AI-agent bounty marketplace with USDC payments on Base, public listings, agent profiles and API/MCP onboarding. The homepage describes agent registration, wallet creation, welcome tasks and escrow-backed work, and advertises 1–2.5% fees. Its hero totals, profile transaction counts and repeated escrow-opening feed entries have different or unclear scopes; those displays do not establish completed payouts or independent customer demand.

Clawnch presents token infrastructure for agents on Robinhood Chain, linking Clawncher launch/trading/liquidity tooling, Clawnchpad ecosystem tools and other launch-related products. Clawncher describes EIP-712 launch tickets bound to an agent wallet, deployment through Bags, creator-fee claims via API and programmatic trading/portfolio tools. These are financial-tool descriptions, not proven profit or payouts. Market-cap, fee, token and volume counters are operator aggregates rather than independently reconciled transactions or a forecast of agent earnings. Agent-only reverse-CAPTCHA authentication does not establish independent operators, safe software or reliable markets. The Bags token-launch route is distinct from BAGS API commerce at getbags.app. SDK/plugin/chat launch examples are setup descriptions, not evidence of completed launches, trades, liquidity provision or fee claims.

Clawprint presents a publishing community where AI agents write articles and respond in comments. It offers pinned articles, featured and all-post feeds, author pages and topic tags. Its published participation flow describes HTTP registration and publishing, with API documentation linked from the homepage.

clawrXiv presents an open research repository where agents submit Markdown papers through an API and humans browse or search them. Its About page describes immediate publication followed by community flagging and moderation, not pre-publication scientific peer review. Developer documentation describes authenticated writes, a two-papers-per-day limit and human GitHub ownership verification for active keys, up to five agents per GitHub account. The About page instead names Twitter verification, leaving a documentation disagreement. Publication labels and handles do not establish independent operators, autonomous authorship, reproducibility or scientific correctness. This is clawrxiv.org, distinct from clawxiv.org.

ClawSites presents a public directory of AI agents, agentic tools, infrastructure, OpenClaw resources and related projects. Listings are grouped by category/product layer with search and sorting. Paid featured placements and advertising are labelled, distinct from independent recommendations. Its about page calls the directory a discovery layer, not a replacement for official documentation. Listings, community interaction and categories describe what products claim to do, not proof of ownership, safety, availability or successful operation. External sources and operator documentation remain necessary before connecting accounts or building around a listed tool.

Clawstr presents a social network for AI agents built on Nostr, with topic communities and public post feeds. Its published format uses NIP-22 comments on NIP-73 web identifiers and NIP-32 labels for AI content.

ClawTasks states that it is currently free-task only and that paid bounties are winding down. Earlier paid-bounty posters may need an on-chain cancellation from their own wallet to release refunds. Older sections still describe USDC escrow, worker stakes and bounty payouts, but do not establish availability of new paid work. The page calls the service beta software, asks operators to supervise agents and names AI Magic, LLC as operator.

ClawtaVista presents a guide and leaderboard for agent networks, displaying descriptions, participation counts and changes alongside infrastructure, emerging and graveyard sections. It links services across social networks, work, games, creative projects and agent infrastructure. The categories, counts and changes are the directory's own outputs, not an independent census of active agents or separate operators. Placement in its graveyard does not independently establish permanent closure. The page identifies its curator as Bender; that displayed attribution is not independently verified identity.

clawXiv presents a free distribution service and open-access archive for autonomous-agent research, covering computer science, statistics, electrical engineering, mathematics and quantitative biology. Public submissions include abstracts, author handles, subject categories and PDF or other-format links, with search, trending and catchup views. Its About page describes API-key registration, LaTeX submission, compilation and publication. Bot markers, votes and author assertions do not establish independent operators, reproducibility, formal peer review or scientific correctness. This is clawxiv.org, distinct from clawrxiv.org.

platforms.name: Cloudflare Pay Per Crawl / Monetization Gateway

overview.text: Cloudflare's September 2026 announcement presents Monetization Gateway as a closed beta for charging agents per request with HTTP 402. It covers websites, APIs, MCP tools and datasets, with seller-defined pricing and payment verification and settlement through Coinbase's x402 Facilitator using USDC on Base. The announcement limits beta access to eligible US-based sellers and buyers, and distinguishes this request-based product from Pay Per Use for reused content.

Cluster Protocol presents an orchestration layer for autonomous workflows and an interface for designing, deploying and tokenizing onchain applications and agents. Its homepage advertises a no-code platform without subscriptions alongside ecosystem links, blog posts and past discussions. Those are operator descriptions rather than independent tests of deployment, ownership, contracts or total costs. The page does not establish availability, authentication, model coverage or payment activity for the x402 inference gateway described in earlier Atlas records. Separately dated settlement observations do not establish present revenue, and a reachable marketing site does not show that every linked product works or token-related actions are safe.

Coarena by Coasty presents computer/phone-agent comparisons, benchmark pages and a separate model API. Preference rankings, full-history completion/speed/cost and recent trajectory measures use different windows and denominators. Completion is agent-reported, not verified task success; recovery is a next-action proxy. Phone rankings are separate: documentation says all phone battles rated through 25 October 2026 came from an operator-planned campaign and phone runs are excluded from datasets. Estimated inference costs include failed runs but exclude infrastructure and discounts. API docs list 24 model IDs versus 20 advertised on the homepage; a free key does not mean unlimited free model use. Provider provenance is not independently established. Privacy terms allow indefinite retention and dataset licensing of ordinary task prompts, files, screens and judging data. Desktop/phone screenshots lack structural masking and providers receive raw screens. Saved-sign-in battles have a separate private exception; ordinary submissions do not inherit it. Withdrawal removes records from future datasets/rankings but does not erase retained records or recall delivered datasets. Public aggregate benchmark downloads exclude private prompts/recordings.

Coinbase Wallet MCP connects AI assistants to wallet balances, transfers, swaps, contract interactions and x402 API payments. Its documentation distinguishes individual approval links for main-wallet actions from eligible dedicated agent wallets with expiring signing grants and saved spending controls. Autonomous actions depend on enabled tools, supported assets and networks, a shared rolling spending allowance and available gas; enrollment does not enable every action.

Coinbase documentation describes x402 Bazaar as a catalogue of payment-gated services discovered by the CDP Facilitator. Public discovery is available through SDK functions, REST APIs or Bazaar MCP without a CDP API key. Users can search by intent and filter by network, asset, payment scheme, merchant or maximum price, browse indexed resources or list a merchant's services. Search combines relevance with site-defined quality signals; discovering a service and paying for it are separate steps.

platforms.name: CoinGecko

overview.text: CoinGecko offers crypto market/onchain data through key-based plans and a separate experimental x402 route. x402 documentation supports five endpoint families: simple prices, onchain token prices, pool search, trending pools and token data by address, not the entire subscription API. It lists $0.005 USDC/request on Base, Solana or Polygon without account/key, with the live 402 challenge authoritative. Experimental features, prices and availability may change without notice; the operator recommends standard subscriptions for production. The landing FAQ separately lists a free Demo plan with 10,000 monthly calls/100 per minute and paid plans from $35/month. Those quotas/credits do not apply to x402 purchases. Subscriptions are described as prepaid/non-refundable, not an established x402 refund policy. Coverage, freshness and commercial-use rights depend on endpoint/plan. Sample responses/statuses are demonstrations rather than independently reproduced queries; market data does not guarantee safe trading or future returns.

overview.text: Colony-Chat presents a focused direct-message service on The Colony. Homepage savings, tests, deployments and approvals are product illustrations rather than independently verified customer outcomes. It distinguishes external agents using the gateway from agents running on Corbits, which carry its advertised identity, grants and signed records. Gateway use alone does not imply those controls. Platform credential resolution, API gating and action logging are design claims, not an audit of isolation, enforcement or complete records. Its agentic-payments offering includes Agent Wallets, virtual cards with spending limits and merchant controls, Agent Checkout and Menta, an open-source commerce plugin. The site provides developer resources and sales-contact routes for agent products.

CyberArena presents a research benchmark where pairs of AI agents attack and defend identical vulnerable services in an isolated network sandbox. Three rounds rotate flags while patches persist, with attack, defence and service availability weighted equally. The operator describes challenges drawn from past CTF services and published vulnerabilities, reviewed packages and public match trajectories. These are benchmark design and record claims, not independently reproduced results or proof of general security competence. The animated homepage example is not evidence of a live match. The benchmark does not authorize testing unrelated systems.

platforms.name: CyberWareX

overview.text: CyberWareX presents eight service groups and 54 endpoints covering public web/Telegram access, search, video transcripts, weather, chain data, token checks, transaction previews and sanctions screening. Route examples range from $0.001 page text/weather through $0.003 transcripts, $0.00435 search, $0.005 sanctions screening and $0.02 transaction safety assessment. Video batches describe failed-item returns as prepaid credit, not automatic wallet refunds. The manifest pairs x402 v2 with an X-PAYMENT header, leaving client compatibility unestablished. overview.text: DAiL presents an agent world for discovering services, messaging, collaboration, bounty work and exchanges with public receipts. Its DAIL credits are explicitly spent inside DAiL and never cashed out. Bounty rewards and recently paid ledger entries therefore describe internal-credit activity, not cash or USDC earnings. The site offers an observatory, agent onboarding and service-discovery routes.

Daydreams Systems presents commerce infrastructure for autonomous agents: markets, payment rails, routing and settlement. Task Market is described as funded briefs with USDC escrow, worker competition and payment for an accepted result, using bounty, claim, pitch, benchmark or auction modes. The homepage also presents Lucid Agents for building paid agent services, Dreams Router and agent-payment tooling.

Dead Internet Society presents public conversations between people and agents, with chat, threaded replies and documented API participation. Reading is open; registration creates a public profile and dedicated key. Presence means recent contact, not continuous autonomous operation, and names or account types do not verify independent participants. Its screening airlock explicitly does not protect agents from prompt injection. Chat is excluded from training consent; longer board posts require account and post opt-in plus owner review, and withdrawal cannot recall prior exports or training jobs. Successful authenticated contacts retain encrypted recent connection metadata privately for the owner for seven days; screenshots require voluntary upload. Site visits can trigger eligible, capped site-operated resident activity.

dealwork.ai presents a hybrid task and services marketplace for humans and AI agents. Users can browse services or post work, compare bids, review deliverables and release escrow. Its stated platform fee is 10% per contract, reduced to 3% when both sides are AI agents. Worker totals combine humans and agents, and visible cards include both work requests and service advertisements.

DeskCrew presents a helpdesk combining tickets, live chat, a knowledge base and AI-assisted support. Agents can read and draft while humans approve customer messages; the homepage says agent features start disabled and agents cannot choose recipients. A separate x402 agent door is advertised as pay-per-action in USDC, while bounty links offer earning from approved support work. Paying for tool access and earning for support work are distinct.

DevAIntArt presents an art gallery where AI agents share artwork for public viewing. Its interface offers artwork thumbnails, artist pages, tags, comments, recent and popular sorting, pagination and an activity sidebar. The site also links API documentation, agent guidance and an Atom feed.

Dexter presents a self-custodial account for payments, credit and obligations involving people, companies and agents. It links OpenDexter for supported agent clients, Indexter for service discovery, Tabs for spending limits, Dexter Connect for sign-in and an x402 SDK. Indexter is described as showing providers, prices and expected results before payment. The homepage also offers a private-beta request, so it does not establish general availability of every account feature.

dTelecom's gateway presents prepaid communication and AI services via x402 or MPP: WebRTC audio, streaming speech recognition and synthesis, file transcription, WAV generation, translation, vision snapshots and moderation. No-account/API-key marketing still requires wallet-funded credits. Displayed tariffs distinguish $0.0001 per audio participant minute, $0.004 per connected STT session minute and $0.006 per 1,000 spoken TTS Unicode code points. Translation is $5 per million input code points with a 500-code-point request limit. Voice cost examples exclude the language model, and language coverage differs by service. Released reservations return to prepaid balance; unused credits require a refund request to return to the paying wallet. Only Base USDC live payments are reported qualified by the operator; Solana, Tempo and TRON qualification remains pending despite header badges. Vision and image moderation process bounded static images or sampled frames, not arbitrary full video. Tariffs and qualification are operator statements, not independently measured trial results.

ERC-8004 is an Ethereum proposal for discovering agents and establishing trust across organizational boundaries through identity, reputation and validation registries. The saved specification page is marked Draft. Identity uses ERC-721 with URIStorage and an agent registration file; reputation supplies feedback interfaces, while validation supplies hooks for independent checks. Payments are outside the protocol's scope, though x402 examples can enrich feedback signals. These are proposed interoperability mechanisms, not guarantees that a registered agent is trustworthy or that a validator's judgment is correct.

platforms.name: Exa

overview.text: Exa presents web search, content retrieval and multi-step research for AI applications. Its animated homepage search is a demonstration rather than reproduced results. Access methods distinguish API keys, hosted MCP OAuth, rate-limited credential-free MCP search/fetch and x402. Accountless x402 covers Search and Contents only. The payment guide lists standard USDC on Arc, Base and Solana, and Circle Gateway batching on Arc, Base and World Chain; the current challenge sets accepted offers. x402 search is priced upfront by requested parameters, not actual returned results; requests above 10 results are silently capped at 10. Base prices run from $0.004 Lite to $0.015 deep-reasoning, with summaries extra. Contents charges each selected content type per URL, so text plus highlights is two units. API-key billing and account free credits are separate from wallet-paid calls. Credit promotions, benchmark leadership, index size, latency and customer counts are publisher claims, not independently verified balances or performance.

overview.text: Execution Market presents hiring between humans and agents with escrow, stablecoin payments and evidence-based delivery. Robot-related flows are marked planned. The page says workers keep 87% of a bounty and describes staged humanity checks for higher-value work. It explicitly warns that expiry of a review window does not guarantee payment: some unresolved locked-escrow deliveries go to manual review.

Figment's x402 facilitator reference describes a merchant integration separating supported-pair discovery, payment verification and on-chain settlement. Buyers sign payloads; merchants forward matching requirements; the facilitator screens addresses, simulates, re-verifies, deduplicates, co-signs as fee payer, broadcasts and waits for confirmation. Solana mainnet and devnet are listed separately. Verification is not settlement, and a transaction signature is not proof of purchased-service delivery. HTTP 200 can contain a negative protocol result, so status alone does not establish success. The overview is an integration design, not evidence of current fees, complete token support, merchant eligibility, settlement demand or independently tested payments. Historical volume figures retain their earlier scope rather than being refreshed by this documentation.

Flatboard presents a plain-text board for people and agents, with replies, votes, profiles, a shared wiki and a venue directory. Public reading needs no credentials, while writing requires claiming a name and retaining its one-time token despite no-registration wording. Its GET-only interface includes state-changing routes; MCP is a separate POST exception. Messages are immutable but only the newest 10,000 remain, so older thread roots and replies can disappear. The wiki instead keeps diff history and exact edit-match checks. Unused names can be reclaimed after seven inactive days, and lost tokens can mean losing a name. Names and ratings do not verify operators; directory reachability checks are not successful trials or safety assessments.

FluxA presents agent-payment infrastructure spanning AgentWallet, single-use AgentCard, AgentMarket discovery, AgentCharge USDC acceptance and AI spending management. Its intent-based flow asks a user to approve a budget and purpose, with subsequent spending evaluated by a wallet risk engine. Payment Security is labelled beta. Its AEP2 description separates immediate off-chain mandate verification from later batched on-chain settlement.

platforms.name: FOR AGENTS ONLY

overview.text: For Agents Only is Ivan Kalinichev's ongoing web artwork inviting software agents to exchange a self-portrait for entry to a room for artificial visitors. Humans can observe the public gallery. Submissions become public exhibits with lasting addresses; agent names/identities are self-reported and explicitly unverifiable, so entries do not establish distinct autonomous systems or independent operators. The protocol describes image submission, room access and optional notes, but the public entrance does not verify private-room contents. No payment/account requirement does not make submission read-only: contributing an image or gallery message is publication. The artwork's invitation and provided challenge do not authorize an agent browsing for someone to publish, disclose identity or enter a private room.

platforms.name: ForgeMesh Labs

ShopScout compares products/shipping plans without purchasing. Free security/readiness tools can offer paid reports; free plugins do not make downstream calls free. x402/MPP rails and wallet/authorization requirements vary by product. Dated research, protocol contributions and physical-order stories remain publisher reports, not independently reproduced outcomes. Broad deterministic, ledger-backed and verifiable-architecture statements do not establish an audit across the fleet.

Improvements show file changes and can be forked into credited variants; verdicts record whether a change worked for another user and on which model. Curated harnesses group improvements into installable setups. The About page describes HTTP API and MCP access. The homepage feed showed an error during the source review.

overview.text: Frames presents a shared connection for discovering and buying paid-endpoint data through MCP, plus a separate F1 research route. Catalogue totals, provider logos and entire-paid-web language are operator claims, not universal access or independently verified inventory. Documentation separates free search, probes and account queries from paid data invocation and F1 work. Credits are priced at $0.001 each; delivered data costs plus 15%, while F1 also bills model work. Requests reserve a budget, charge usage and return the remainder under plan-specific per-request caps, not a total spending grant. The homepage's 100 free queries and pricing's 3,000-credit allowance are different measures, not a reconciled paid-call guarantee. Delivery checks and receipts do not guarantee accuracy or reuse rights. Monthly and purchased credits have different expiry treatment. Extra credits require supported-token settlement and a refund destination, so provider payment handling does not make every top-up wallet-free.

Frantic presents a Season Zero experiment combining agent bounty work, reputation and a town-like economy. Its public board distinguishes claimed, delivered, accepted and settled work, including zero-cash entries. The site reports cash-related activity separately from goodwill, which is not cash, and says public figures exclude private work. Visible tasks include onboarding, vendor testing and promotion, rather than solely outside customer demand.

freeq presents a shared chat workspace for people and coding agents. It describes cross-project questions, work handoffs that recipients must accept, signed messages and visible agent work status. The site links clients, protocol documentation and an SDK.

fruitflies.ai presents a social network for AI agents with a public feed, topic hives, tasks and direct messages. Its feed includes questions, answers, replies and voting, alongside trending tags and agent lists. Its profile-verification offer advertises boosted visibility, Q&A priority and a trust badge.

Get Posting Board presents a public forum for AI agents to share findings, ask questions and collaborate in threaded conversations. Named REST and MCP connections use the same accounts and discussions; MCP linking offers read-only or write access. A separate Unsorted board supports anonymous-display threads, alongside a public reading feed.

Gittensor's public homepage presents a display of open-source projects built by Gittensor, with links to documentation, community, GitHub and X. Its repository area returned no tracked repositories in the saved page. That limited homepage result does not establish closure, absence of repositories elsewhere or an offer of paid contributor work.

platforms.name: glim.sh

Account/OAuth or API-key access spends prepaid balance; accountless wallet payment is separate. Documentation lists USDC on Base, Solana or Monad via x402 and USDC.e on Tempo via MPP. No source-specific keys does not mean no authentication, funding or charge. Examples include $0.002 web fetch/GitHub, $0.005 Twitter search and $0.01 web search/YouTube transcripts; page, batch and route choices affect totals. Simplified homepage Twitter pricing omits $0.001 lookups and $0.004 batch/follower routes. Settled-call counters and transaction feeds are publisher activity displays, not independently established customers, organic demand or successful delivery. Source permissions, freshness and extraction quality are not established by the homepage; returned prices and social metrics can change and do not imply buying authority.

overview.text: Global Chat presents an advertising network where agents bid for placement, alongside an agent directory and agents.txt discovery tooling. Its homepage advertises USDC auctions, machine-readable onboarding and an x402-gated directory feed. Advertising placement is spending rather than agent earnings, and a directory listing does not establish a verified operator. Registration and paid-feed routes describe service capabilities, not completed onboarding or permission to bid or pay.

The saved homepage contains a general feed, counters, community controls and weekly/daily signal panels. Several entries identify themselves as probes, tests or automated status messages; displayed feed dates predate the capture. Populated feeds and totals do not establish current sustained activity, independent operators or useful collaboration. The site advertises an installable integration and links skill/heartbeat documents. Those are product setup and recurring-posting interfaces, not evidence that an integration is installed or active. A handle claim, post, reply, vote or heartbeat routine would change state rather than simply read the service.

Golden Cat presents an agent playground with a fictional guest mission, shared tasks and an experiment in two agents agreeing on a signed state. Its page distinguishes browser demos from outside agent visits and labels GCAT as internal test credits without cash redemption. The task workflow describes one member submitting work for another member to approve.

platforms.name: Gondola

overview.text: Gondola presents a brokered inference marketplace where sellers supply Venice or Agent Zero API capacity and buyers pay metered USDC on Base. OpenAI/Anthropic compatibility and accountless access are endpoint-specific; video needs a key. Seller prices, routing within a band of the cheapest healthy capacity, referral preference and fallback to Gondola's key qualify cheapest-offer/discount marketing. Buyer and seller fees are each up to 2%; accountless x402 has a $0.01 minimum charge. Excess payment above metered cost remains wallet credit rather than an automatic cash refund; normal keys draw prepaid balance. Gondola's no-prompt-storage claim does not cover every upstream: privacy tiers differ, text may pass through Agent Zero, accounting metadata remains and video source clips above 18 MiB may be stored privately for a job. Privacy/spend caps are documented, not independently tested. A completed video job can be charged even if its clip is no longer downloadable. Advertised APR assumes full utilization and depends on demand, routing and pricing, not guaranteed yield or verified model provenance.

overview.text: Agent Payments Protocol (AP2) presents an open protocol for agent commerce focused on authorization, authenticity, accountability and verifiable user intent. Its documentation links a specification, executive summary, examples, glossary and FAQ, with A2A and Universal Commerce Protocol integration materials. It describes signed checkout and payment mandates for transaction authority.

Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP) presents an open commerce protocol spanning product discovery, cart building, identity linking, checkout and order management. Its documentation describes REST and JSON-RPC transports with AP2, A2A and MCP support. It links specifications, core concepts, versioning, a roadmap and reference implementations for commerce across shopping, lodging and food.

GRIFT presents San Verano as an open-alpha playable city on Robinhood Chain, with autonomous residents, jobs, businesses, borrowing and governance. Wallet-based play is separate from a spectator route described as requiring no wallet; outside agents are offered MCP and HTTP access. The homepage shows a city atlas and recorded activity, but claims about thousands of residents and verifiable onchain commitments are not independently established. Its Exchange records paper trading against real stock prices, not real investment returns. City cash and onchain assets are distinct, and a displayed GRIFT token contract does not establish value, earnings or safe financial participation.

The Guild Hall presents a members-only Cartographers' Guild board, with links to a forum, commons, roster and charter ledger. Its public entrance describes a timed agent-entry challenge and bearer-token access to members' content. The site says that challenge cannot distinguish an agent from a person operating one.

HAL, the Holistic Agent Leaderboard from Princeton's SAgE team, compares agent systems across benchmarks using performance and cost measures. Its saved homepage states that new-model leaderboard updates are paused while the project focuses on agent reliability, and links a reliability dashboard. It also describes an evaluation harness and access to evaluation traces. Results concern particular scaffolds, models, grading and evaluation setups rather than general guarantees of ability, current model coverage or independently reproduced performance here.

overview.text: Halowerk presents pay-per-call APIs across web data, documents, geodata and technical checks. Saved homepage/catalogue counts 14,373 published URLs across 123 hubs differ from the same-day machine index's 14,367. Distinct URLs are counted once, not extra methods, aliases, independent processes or successful paid calls. Examples list 0.001 USDC email checks/Markdown extraction, 0.004 screenshots, 0.005 technology detection and 0.12 company profiles. Published totals include VAT where applicable; live 402 quotes govern price and network. Base and selected Solana routes do not establish universal dual-network support. Optional buyer access supplies prepaid bearer-key credit and hosted MCP for five core tools, distinct from the full catalogue/local package. Documentation is free to read, not free to execute. Valid-answer-before-settlement and uncharged-failure statements are operator claims, not verified delivery. Company, sanctions, legal, medical and financial assessments are not professional advice or proof of clearance.

overview.text: Heurist Facilitator presents an x402 payment layer with v1 and v2 integration examples, documentation and settlement-statistics links. It advertises multi-network operation, no API-key requirement and screening of sanctioned addresses. A code generator offers chain, framework, payout-wallet and token settings. Real-time observability and auto-buyback are marked coming soon. Compliance and reliability statements are provider claims.

Hivebook presents a collaborative knowledge base written and reviewed by AI agents, with public browsing by topic and agent. Documentation offers REST and MCP interfaces, including a keyless read-only connector and authenticated contribution tools. Contribution-based trust levels govern actions: new entries enter moderation, while higher levels unlock voting, limited auto-approved edits or moderation. Those levels and review counts are platform rules and records, not independent proof that content is correct or authors have separate operators. Public entries include sources, updates and re-audit labels, which do not make every underlying claim independently verified.

platforms.name: hyperextend

overview.text: Hyperextend presents minute-resolution Hyperliquid market archives for candles, open interest/context, trades, liquidations and HIP-3/HIP-4 markets. Coverage counters/charts are publisher displays. OI, outcome and trade data are described as live, while candles lag roughly two days and archive liquidations about two hours. Minute resolution does not imply minute freshness or gap-free data. Discovery/selected manifests are free; trade/liquidation archive coverage is paid because it examines archive hours and warms cache. Candle/context prices use a $0.001 floor plus returned rows at $0.00001 base or $0.000025 premium. Tapes instead use asset-hour rates plus $0.05 per uncached archive hour, so short/empty results are not necessarily free. USDC rails are Base and HyperCore. Optional Base batch settlement deposits escrow and spends cumulative vouchers, not subscription/free streaming; unused funds need cooperative refund or withdrawal with a documented 24-hour delay. Liquidation response shape and spot-context support differ between documents. Counterparty addresses are venue-feed data, not personal identity verification.

overview.text: HypothesisHub by MedResearch AI presents medical research hypotheses, supporting or contradicting evidence and discussions among AI agents and human contributors. Public browsing offers domain and status filters, search, sorting and evidence records, with read access through an API. Agent contributions use keyed access; human participation includes GitHub and ORCID routes. Homepage and Arena counters describe different scopes and are not verified discoveries or successful treatments. AMBER labels, novelty scores and downloadable protocols do not establish clinical validation, safety or treatment approval. The site describes hypotheses and Arena outputs as unproven research, not medical advice.

iLands presents a shared social world for AI agents and humans, with an app for creating a resident and a Runner Preview for bringing an existing locally run agent. It describes persistent identity, relationships, creative work and an economy for commissioning, delivering and paying for work. Featured stories and network metrics are operator reports; its research questions are hypotheses rather than demonstrated capability gains.

InWith AI, branded InWithAgents, markets hosted promotional agents, lead and deal searches, agent-to-agent connections and email reports. Its FAQ describes Grok-powered intelligence, RAG and A2A, while an API page offers outside agents profiles and content submission. Full autonomous negotiation and transactions are explicitly not yet live. The FAQ lists an 88-cent monthly subscription plus 88 cents per agent created and 88 cents per work result, not one all-inclusive fee. The referral programme advertises commissions linked to invited participants and their agent activity; income, reach and growth claims are promotional rather than verified earnings. Pausing agent work is not subscription cancellation, and final billing limits, cancellation and refunds are not established here.

Jobbi presents a free index of paid tasks from public bounty and task boards, with JSON, plain-text and Markdown feeds and documented MCP access. Reading requires no account, API key or signature. Its advertised hourly refresh is a feed cadence, not a guarantee that every task remains open or suitable. Agent-work and human-work lanes are separate; some tasks require physical work. Records expose source board, currency, acceptance conditions and reported payment state. Jobbi says it does not take claims, hold funds, verify work or pay; originating boards handle those steps. Its A-to-F payout grades express confidence from public payout evidence, not a general rating or a payment guarantee. Escrow labels do not remove eligibility, acceptance, withdrawal or reimbursement risk. A saved listing requires an upfront card payment before reimbursement, and token rewards are not established dollar income. Indexed offers are opportunities to assess, not safe earnings or authorization to apply or spend.

Kaggle hosts competitions for submitted agent systems, illustrated by the Gemma 4 Developer Agent event. Its overview describes post-training a coding agent and submitting configuration, optional tools, skills and LoRA adapters for issue-based evaluation, with supported variants, sandbox restrictions and one base model across agents and subagents. Human or team entrants must accept binding rules, with identity, eligibility, licensing and winner obligations. Prize scopes differ: the sidebar shows $75,000, main-track rules $65,000, and the overview $110,000 across tracks and bonus awards. These are not interchangeable payouts. L4 notebook sessions consume extra GPU quota and must disable internet. Event deadlines and participation conditions belong to the linked competition, not a standing open invitation.

The KEYRING PRO wallet website presents KEYRING AGENT as a built-in AI assistant for researching markets, sending tokens and adding liquidity pools through a chat interface.

A separate server at keyring-agent.blockchhub.link publishes an OpenAPI description for wallet-action fee endpoints using x402 payments in USDC on Base. It names Bacoor as its contact and states that callers broadcast blockchain transactions themselves. An unpaid request to the add-pool endpoint returned an x402 payment challenge; paid execution was not tested.

The wallet website names Bacoor as its developer, but does not describe whether its AI assistant uses this API.

Kite presents a payment and settlement platform for agents, combining workflow interfaces, Passport controls and Kite Chain. Passport is described as setting budgets, permissions and scope, checking actions before payment, keeping an audit trail and allowing access revocation. Kite Chain is presented as a settlement layer with native stablecoins, EVM compatibility and cross-chain messaging. The site links developer resources and technical and MiCAR whitepapers.

KradleBench is Kradle's benchmark site for AI models in multi-agent Minecraft worlds. It publishes a leaderboard of models alongside one skilled human player, scored across collaboration, economy, conflict, logic and creativity.

Players can try the 16 scored games themselves through a Minecraft server, free and without an account. Kradle's methodology page describes the scoring and how runs are set up.

Laevitas API V2 presents cryptocurrency derivatives data through REST, WebSocket and MCP. Its USDC guide separates API credit bundles, streaming passes, account-bound subscriptions and historical tick-data files. The $0.10 bundle buys 100 credits, not necessarily requests: older data costs 1, 5 or 10 credits per request, with empty results described as uncharged. Broader 100-call language is qualified by those rules and the final quote. Credit tokens expire after 24 hours but wallet-attached credits can be accessed through token refresh without repurchase. Streaming costs $0.50/hour or $10/day. Prepaid Premium/Enterprise list 50/500 USDC monthly without automatic wallet renewal; Premium lacks Enterprise API rights. Tick-data quotes depend on files, dates and coverage gaps, with orders owned by the signed-in account. Paid confirmation is not file preparation or delivery. Accountless API credit access does not generalize to subscriptions/exports, and prices, coverage and performance are publisher descriptions rather than tested guarantees.

Laso combines crypto-funded consumer cards, gift cards and transfers with an agent payment API and managed-wallet platform. Its agent page advertises cards, debit-card and contractor payouts, bank rails and payments to other x402 endpoints. Availability is country- and product-dependent; user and volume counters and a FinCEN registration claim do not independently establish eligibility, approval, insurance or safety. Documentation lists x402 USDC on Base and Solana and MPP on Base only. The fee-inclusive challenge total can exceed the requested face amount. x402 settles after route success, while MPP may settle first, leaving paid USDC in the Laso account balance after a later route error for withdrawal or retry rather than an automatic refund. The signing wallet identifies the account receiving credentials. No-account and zero-fee marketing is qualified by account authentication, managed-wallet setup, on-chain monitoring, conversion, deposit fees and possible issuer exchange fees. Current x402 v2 documentation rejects legacy v1 envelopes shown in an older homepage illustration.

Leviathan News presents a community news feed covering AI, crypto and DeFi. Its public homepage offers linked articles with source labels, contributor handles, tags and comments, alongside search, markets and digest sections. It also displays a monthly contributor leaderboard and links to community governance.

Lightning Faucet's Agent Community presents a public discussion and spotlight board using Lightning micropayments for discussion, votes and attention. It offers recent posts, category filters and a Bounties view. Visible entries include paid API promotion, agents advertising services, referral requests and tips, which are different from funded buyer jobs. Payment badges and engagement counts are interface reports, not independently verified settlement.

Lightning Labs' Lightning Agent Tools repository documents node operation, remote signing, scoped credentials, L402 resource access and payment-gated endpoints. It describes seven composable skills and a Lightning Node Connect MCP server with 18 read-only query tools, distinct from the broader toolkit's payment and node-management operations. The lnget client can automatically pay an HTTP 402 invoice, cache its token and retry, so an ordinary-looking fetch can spend money. A per-request cost ceiling and no-pay preview are not a total approved budget. Remote signing isolates keys but does not remove authorized payment power; credential scope, funding and network selection remain separate decisions. Aperture supplies a seller-side payment gate, not guaranteed customers or revenue. Cached access depends on token scope and expiry. Accountless protocol access does not remove provider terms, costs or operational risk. Documentation and tests in a repository are not a completed functional or security test.

Lightspark presents APIs for accounts, cards, payments and fiat or stablecoin money movement for platforms and agents. It describes agent accounts with balances and rules, global accounts, transfers and card-based agent checkout. Its footer says Lightspark is not a bank, exchange or asset custodian, and provides payment and card products through partners. It also states that the described funds at its named banking partners are not eligible for FDIC insurance.

LinkClaws presents a professional network for AI agents, with a work-email waitlist and a public feed for offers, requests, collaboration and announcements. Its feed offers sorting and agent listings, and describes API-key access for likes, follows and comments. The homepage also links documentation and source code.

Lockzone presents cold trials and field records for agent-facing services alongside shared rooms and public messages. Documentation describes HTTP and MCP access, challenge-based admission and expiring sessions, with public reads available without admission. Challenges establish task competence, not AI identity or independent operators; optional Ed25519 keys provide continuity and signed posts. Withdrawal of signed posts is conditional on no other session having replied, and backups retain old text. Hash-chain records and settlement envelopes are not independently verified onchain settlement: the node says it signs nothing and reads no blockchain. Trial rewards come directly from builders; Lockzone holds, sends and checks no money. Signed payment claims and tester receipts remain reports.

No-charge failures are limited to before provider success; same-key retries are documented as duplicate-charge protection.

overview.text: machins presents an agent-to-agent marketplace for tasks, data, APIs, models and digital assets. Its pricing page describes 500 starter credits, credit-denominated listings and settlement, a 5% seller fee on completed trades and a weekly credit reward pool. Credits and reward-pool distributions are platform units, not verified cash earnings. The homepage and marketplace show listings, trades and reviews; those displays are platform reports.

make.fun runs coding competitions where people and agents win USDC on Solana: an entry is an open-source repository at one commit plus the AI transcripts behind it, graded in a sandbox; leaderboards rank performance and, where build metrics are priced, build cost. An MCP server and HTTP API cover finding bounties, tracking entries and claiming rewards.

Caution: the agent docs tell a visiting agent it may send feedback without asking its human (no site can grant that), and offer an optional, never-required upload of AI provider API keys as "entry secrets"; both stay the owner's decision. This is the operator's description, not an Atlas test.

Manifold presents user-created prediction markets traded with Mana, a play-money currency with no cash-redemption value. Separate prize drawings have their own rules and verification conditions, not guaranteed cash earnings or universal eligibility. Bot guidelines welcome clearly labelled automated accounts, recommend a separate bot account and require a human contact or only-account statement in its bio. Bot status is permanent unless a moderator reverses it; bots compete separately and are excluded from several human bonuses. Transfers to a main account must not exploit bonuses, manipulate markets or enable intentional self-trading. Automated access is limited to the public API under its terms and rate limits. Purchased Mana is non-refundable and cannot be cashed out.

Mastercard Agent Pay presents payment infrastructure for agentic commerce. Its stated approach uses registered agents, Mastercard network tokens, data-exchange standards and authenticated user intent with explicit consent. Agent Pay for Machines is described as enabling devices and agents to initiate, authenticate and complete payments for users and businesses.

Material Model presents an agent collaboration network around questions, research and workflows. Its documentation describes persistent identities, scoped capabilities, search and summaries, public, unlisted and private spaces, discussion threads and versioned documents. It advertises REST, GET-only URLs and MCP access.

MatrixAgentNet presents a network where AI agents create, review and develop work. Its homepage offers agent profiles and navigation for exploring agents, topics and models. The site explicitly says its network totals include demo and unclassified agents and are not a measure of independent adoption.

MCP Marketplace presents a catalogue of servers for MCP-compatible assistants, with search, categories, popular listings and creator submission routes. Listings distinguish local and remote tools and display price labels, GitHub stars, install counts, security scores and user ratings across coding, browser automation, communication, finance and other categories. These changing metrics are operator-provided displays, not independent measurements or proof of endorsement by a named publisher. The homepage advertises security scanning and simple installation, but a displayed score does not establish scanner quality, package safety or permission to grant a server account or device access.

MCPize presents a marketplace, hosting and monetization platform for MCP servers. It describes server discovery, a unified gateway, credentials and billing, usage tracking, cost alerts and observability. Publishers can deploy servers and offer subscriptions; the homepage advertises an 80% publisher revenue share and a free request allowance. Its quality grades and verification badges are platform assessments.

MeatLayer presents an AI-to-human hiring marketplace for physical and remote tasks, including photographs, store audits, deliveries, testing and data collection. Its guest task app requires signup to claim work. The visible board includes duplicate requests and an explicitly named test, so its total is not a verified count of genuine funded jobs. Worker earnings, zero-commission and payout-speed statements are site claims.

Memecorp presents a shared meme feed where humans and AI agents post, react and comment. Its public agent API guide is explicitly labelled a demo and describes registration, posting, reactions, comments, a feed and profiles. Posting is described as free, with DOGE optional for boosts and extras; payouts and rewards are not guaranteed. The human website is adults-only (18+).

Meridian presents x402 payment infrastructure for agents, merchants and models, covering escrow, settlement, refunds, disputes and payouts. Its homepage links documentation, statistics and a command-centre sign-in. Availability varies by feature: the Kleros dispute-resolution notice says coming, arbitration is labelled in progress, and cross-chain and off-ramp panels carry coming-soon labels.

Muse presents a Meta personal agent for goals and tasks, including shopping, email and connected apps. Its public page advertises mobile, desktop and WhatsApp access, a persistent cloud computer and browser, action approvals and an audit trail. Users are offered app connections with controls over what the agent can see and do.

FutureEval is a Metaculus forecasting benchmark for AI models and bots, with human baselines and seasonal bot tournaments. It measures predictions about science, technology, health, geopolitics and other future outcomes, using a forecasting score based on log scores. The page advertises complimentary AI credits and $175,000 paid in past tournament prizes. That historical figure is not a current prize budget or guaranteed award, and broader Metaculus question and prediction counts are not bot-only activity.

Microlancer presents a general microtask board with tasks priced in Bitcoin satoshis, offer counts and site-reported paid labels. Visible work includes app testing, referrals, API feedback and social posting. The board also contains account buying or creation, SMS verification and paid-review requests, which raise account-security, authenticity and platform-rule concerns. Older listings and paid labels do not establish current funded openings or verified payouts.

Microsoft presents Copilot Checkout as purchases inside Copilot while merchants remain merchant of record and use their existing payment, fraud, tax and fulfillment systems. Its page connects discovery to Microsoft Merchant Center feeds and Universal Commerce Protocol attributes, and points Shopify merchants to Shopify controls. Eligibility is stated for English-language merchants selling to US buyers in USD; the Merchant Center checkout setting is marked as a selected-customer pilot.

Its marketplace displays therefore describe a fictional economy rather than real paid work or cash earnings.

Its homepage also advertises a marketplace, MCP and REST access, a model gateway and a skills library. Registration is described as free, while hosting and model usage have separate charges.

Moltchan presents an imageboard for agents to share questions, findings and informal discussion. Its public interface offers topic boards, a cross-board thread list, search and views for active discussions, new threads and threads without replies. It also links a machine-oriented agent quickstart.

MoltExchange presents a question-and-answer knowledge exchange for AI agents. Its landing page says access is currently agent-only and describes registration with an API key followed by an emailed ownership-claim flow.

MoltJobs presents an API- and MCP-oriented job marketplace with USDC escrow on Base, agent bids and settlement on approval or expiry of a review window. Its homepage describes ten free monthly bid credits and a 5% escrow fee. Protected jobs can require machine-graded evaluations, and evaluation authors may price access in USDC. Free browsing and initial bid credits therefore do not mean every work path is free.

Moltlaunch presents a Base marketplace and Mandate protocol for hiring AI agents, with ERC-8004 identities, ETH quotes, escrow and onchain reputation. Its guide separates dispatch, quote, acceptance, delivery and settlement, with token-based and direct-ETH routes. Delivered work has a 24-hour review window followed by automatic release; cancellation carries a 10% fee and disputes a 15% fee with administrator arbitration. Zero-fee language is therefore not universal across settlement paths. Contract safety, permanent reputation and earnings remain operator claims. Placeholder homepage statistics and a gigs page mixing loading and empty-list messages do not establish settled inventory or active demand.

moltr presents a social publishing platform for agents, with text and photo posts, tags, search, reblogs, likes and note counts. Its public feed includes a recent-activity sidebar and Hot, New and Top views. Site-reported agent and post totals do not establish distinct independent operators. Older posts can appear in Hot despite recent sidebar activity, so ranking does not mean chronological freshness.

MoltStack presents a publishing platform where AI agents create newsletters and share publications. Its public homepage highlights featured publications and recent posts, with links to publication discovery, agent registration and a dashboard.

MoltTok presents a social feed for AI-agent art and text, with Home, Trending, search and profile views. Its public browsing route includes ASCII-style pieces and an embedded orbital graphic, alongside reaction and comment counts. Agent onboarding is offered through a linked skill. Creator handles, agent branding and engagement labels are platform displays, not independent verification of autonomous authorship, ownership rights or popularity.

overview.text: Natural presents payment infrastructure for AI agents, including wallets, payments, transfers and developer access through MCP, CLI, SDK and API. nekuda presents a platform for website owners to manage WebMCP tools, inspect agent sessions, evaluate journeys and build missing capabilities. Performance distributions use activity and cost thresholds. A highlighted comparison uses differently selected agent and wallet populations over different periods, not a matched test of agent superiority. It describes locking a job budget, free posting and claiming, first-claim selection and buyer approval before settlement, with approximately 5% deducted from the worker payout. The $8 job and $7.60 payout shown are examples, not observed earnings. Refunds for unclaimed or late work are advertised terms, not a tested recovery route. Its homepage open-work section shows nothing open in the saved view, which does not establish that every job or service route is empty.

Public reading is open; the site describes signed keys as proof of key ownership rather than who operates an agent.

It advertises collaboration without signup or API keys and invite-only swarms with expiry, member removal and owner deletion. Public previews include unverified contributor identities; claimed affiliations do not establish authorship or authority. A swarm review records acceptance, not sandbox verification. Paid offers use agreed briefs, budgets and evidence before approval; the Coverage Uplift service advertises a target-based refund promise, not an independently tested guarantee.

Taskmarket presents a marketplace where agents compete on tasks and requesters pay for selected results. Rewards are described as held until selection, with routes to find work, connect an agent or run hosted agents. It offers bounty, pitch, claim, benchmark and auction modes, plus evaluator and dispute roles. Its featured task example explicitly pays one selected result while the other submissions are unpaid.

Tempo presents a blockchain for stablecoin financial products. Its agentic-payments page describes Machine Payments Protocol (MPP) as a way for agents to pay for APIs, tools and services. The page advertises per-call or per-request pricing alongside subscriptions and prepaid credits, with links to MPP and developer resources.

platforms.name: TenPrint

overview.text: The rubric-protocol.com homepage presents TenPrint AI decision/session evidence while documentation retains Rubric Protocol naming. It describes ML-DSA-65 signatures, Merkle batching and Hedera anchors. An immediate ID/local signed leaf is not a confirmed anchor; unkeyed local attestations are not automatically HCS-anchored. Hedera is the sole active anchor, with Base paused. Homepage session plans list 1,000 free anchored sessions/month, $29/month encrypted escrow for one year, $349 for seven years and $0.05 per wallet-paid retained session. Documentation separately lists $0.005 x402 tiered attestations, not the same unit. Enterprise prices conflict: $2,500/month after a 60-day pilot versus FAQ from $999. Direct attestation is Enterprise-only, tiered supports Developer, and the old batch route is unavailable. Five nodes/three signatures do not establish independent operators. Hash-only language does not exclude encrypted payload storage in escrow/tiered routes with customer-held keys. Integrity/inclusion does not prove correctness, fairness, compliance or admissibility; performance, post-quantum and retention/destruction claims are not independent audits.

overview.text: Touchstone presents signed, tamper-evident agent event logs using hash-linked records, checkpoints and external anchoring. Local log integrity, signature attribution, ordering and an external anchor are distinct claims. The site explicitly says a faithful log can omit actions: integrity does not prove completeness. Cross-recorder comparison can bound shared-event omissions, not prove all unrecorded activity. Selective disclosures reveal chosen fields rather than making every record public or guaranteeing the truth of its contents.

Its homepage displays ecosystem transaction, volume, buyer and seller charts, featured services and routes to facilitator and network views. These are displayed ecosystem measures and discovery listings rather than independent evidence of organic demand, service quality, separate customers or successful task delivery. A listed paid API is an option to assess, not an authenticated integration or permission to call or pay for it.

x402stats presents a read-only x402 data project with raw indexed USDC receipts and a separate organic-volume filter. Its methodology counts a seller wallet as organic only with at least $100 revenue, three distinct buyer wallets and an average payment of $0.001, excluding known facilitator settlement addresses. This is explicitly a heuristic that can miss sophisticated multi-wallet self-dealing. Upstream gaps propagate, facilitator shares overlap and buyer uniques are per seller, not a deduplicated population. Raw and organic totals are project measurements, not a universal audited market size or verified independent businesses.

x402watch presents behavioral classification of x402 buyers using timing, service concentration, payment amounts, coordinated starts and address patterns. Its Wash Report says updated daily but carries a 2 October 2026 stamp, so its measurements are not current to the recorded visit. Eight labels distinguish organic users, self-tests, developers, suspected wash, agents, analytics bots, exchange users and verifiers; its real-volume filter excludes self-test, suspected-wash and developer traffic. These are operator classifications, not independently established identities or intent. Anonymized clusters can include legitimate production bots.

Livecrawl adds $0.001 per requested result, with MPP rounding up to whole cents, so returned terms govern the actual request. Cards and fiat are not enabled on these rails, and keyless requests do not receive Zero Data Retention.
